title: Trump Administration Suffers Double Legal Setback Over Immigration Rules
summary:
The Trump administration suffered two setbacks to its immigration agenda on Monday as a federal judge halted proposed visa caps and dozens of Democratic-led states launched legal challenges against broader residency restrictions.

A US federal judge blocked the administration from imposing fixed time limits on how long foreign students and journalists can remain in the country without applying for extensions. Under the proposed limitation, F visas for international students and J visas that allow cultural exchange programs would be capped at four years. I visas for journalists, which currently can last for years, would be limited to 240 days.

Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, who was appointed by Republican President George W. Bush, called the Department of Homeland Security's rationale citing national security and the need to prevent fraud "exceptionally weak." He noted that the existing system has allowed tens of millions of scholars to contribute to groundbreaking research and substantial economic expansion, warning that the damage to higher education and the wider US economy would be "catastrophic." The measures would affect roughly 1.6 million international students holding F visas and about 500,000 exchange visitors on J visas.

At the same time, two lawsuits were filed in a Manhattan federal court to derail a separate DHS regulation scheduled to take effect on Friday. The measure seeks to broaden the criteria by which immigration officers can deem applicants inadmissible as a "public charge," a legal standard historically applied to individuals likely to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence. New York, California and Illinois are leading a coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia seeking to block the policy, joined by a parallel suit from six cities and counties.

Under the Biden administration, immigration officers could consider cash aid when evaluating green card applicants but were barred from penalizing the use of non-cash support such as food assistance and Medicaid. The Trump administration is now seeking to revive first-term policies that treat non-cash assistance as a disqualifying factor, while also extending scrutiny to benefits received by an applicant's family members.

A DHS spokesperson defended the regulation, describing the plaintiffs as "left-wing leaders" who were "terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs." In a statement, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the rule "seeks to push immigrant families away from the programs that have kept people fed and healthy for decades." The lawsuits argue that the administration overstepped its legal authority by bypassing Congress, which holds the sole power to set the criteria for permanent residency.
why_it_matters: These two cases test how much power a president has to reshape immigration policy without Congress — decisions that affect millions of students, workers and families, and that set the rules for who gets to live in the United States. They also matter to U.S. universities, cities and local economies that depend on international students, exchange programs and immigrant families.

background_read: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is the U.S. agency in charge of immigration, border control and visas. It issues different visa types: F visas for international students, J visas for exchange visitors such as scholars, and I visas for foreign journalists.

A green card gives someone permanent residency — the right to live and work in the U.S. permanently. Under U.S. law, Congress rather than the president sets the main rules for who can receive one, which is central to the arguments in these lawsuits.

The 'public charge' idea dates back to the 1800s: the government has long said it can turn away people likely to depend on public support. The first Trump administration widened that test so that using food aid or Medicaid could count against an applicant, but federal courts blocked the rule and the Biden administration later dropped it.

Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV, who blocked the visa time limits, was appointed by President George W. Bush, a Republican — a reminder that judges' rulings do not always match the party of the president who chose them.

International students often pay full tuition at U.S. universities and support hundreds of thousands of jobs, which is why universities, businesses and states frequently fight visa restrictions in court.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — universities, exchange programs and immigrant advocates
perspectives.description: Universities and exchange organizations see the visa ruling as protection: the judge warned the damage to higher education and the wider economy would be 'catastrophic,' and students and journalists keep their existing timelines. Cities like New York argue the public charge rule would scare immigrant families away from food aid and Medicaid that keep people fed and healthy.

DHS calls the plaintiffs 'left-wing leaders' who fear losing federal funds, and describes the rules as tools for national security and fraud prevention. From this view, fixed visa time limits and a stronger public charge test are legitimate uses of executive authority, because they push people to support themselves rather than rely on public programs.

Both fights turn on the same structural question: how much immigration policy a president can set without Congress, which holds the power over permanent residency. The 'public charge' test has existed for more than a century, but its reach has swung with each administration — widened under Trump, narrowed under Biden, widened again now — and courts keep having to referee.

The public charge regulation is scheduled to take effect Friday, so a judge's ruling could come within days of the lawsuits being filed. Whatever happens, the cases are likely to move through appeals courts, and the outcomes could shape how far future presidents can go on visas, green cards and benefits.
